tagline: Creek roads, a former lumber railway and spruce-covered heights near Damascus.
intro: Route 91 crosses two forks of the Holston River between Glade Spring and Damascus, then follows Laurel Creek through the Iron Mountains toward Tennessee. Near Whitetop Mountain, Route 600 passes Elk Garden, a gap between Whitetop and Mount Rogers where the Appalachian Trail crosses the road. Virginia's byway program designates scenic roads to introduce travelers to alternative destinations. At Whitetop, red spruce grows at the summit, while beech and maple dominate below 4,700 feet.

The Virginia Creeper Trail follows an old railroad grade from Abingdon to Whitetop. That railway carried lumber from Konnarock, where a sawmill operated from 1906 to 1928. Little of the sawmill remains; near Damascus, Route 91 crosses the rail trail and joins US 58 alongside the creek and trail. The Konnarock sawmill employed more than 400 workers and had 20 logging camps, producing more than 15 million board feet of lumber annually.

Travel south from Glade Spring through Lodi to Damascus, then take US 58 toward the Whitetop area. For the mountain branch, Route 600 links Route 603, Little Laurel Road, with US 58 through Elk Garden. Forest Road 89 branches from Route 600 toward Whitetop's summit, a separate road from the through route.

moments.title: Damascus
moments.text: Damascus brings together travel on foot, bicycle and motorcycle: its five scenic trails include the Appalachian Trail, Virginia Creeper Trail and MABDR motorcycle trail. The town hosts Trail Days each year around the middle of May. The Creeper Trail occupies an old railroad grade whose trains once carried lumber from Konnarock. Road and rail geography meet just outside town, where Route 91 crosses the trail and joins US 58 parallel to Laurel Creek. Damascus suffered flooding and devastation from Hurricane Helene in 2024. The Iron Mountain Trail and U.S. Bicycle Route 76 complete the five-trail convergence.

moments.title: Konnarock
moments.text: Bark shingles cover the main building of Konnarock Training School, a Lutheran girls' school built in 1925. The wood-frame building has a hipped roof and an attached chapel at the rear. The Lutheran church developed the property as a mission to the southern Appalachians. After the school closed in 1958, the Forest Service acquired it. Restored in 2022, it is now used by the Blue Ridge Discovery Center, which specializes in nature education. A chestnut-bark-shingled bungalow built in 1936 originally served as the school's Health Center. The main building rises two and a half stories and extends across 14 bays.
moments.notice: Bark shingles cover the school building, with a chapel attached at the rear.

moments.title: Whitetop Mountain
moments.text: Whitetop supports old-growth red spruce and other northern softwoods more commonly found farther north. It is Virginia's second-highest independent mountain after Mount Rogers, but its third-highest named peak when Mount Rogers' subsidiary Pine Mountain is counted. The mountain hosted the White Top Folk Festival from 1932 to 1939 except in 1937. Beech and maple dominate below 4,700 feet, while red spruce grows at the summit. Forest Road 89 connects the summit with Route 600. Its mountain balds date to the 1800s or earlier and are maintained by prescribed burning every two or three years, depending on conditions.
